Subject: ArgoHealth capacity corridor: SLA fit, token throughput model & slab proposal

Hi Sara —

Following up from last week's call. I attached an initial capacity model (argo_capacity_model_v1.xlsx) with conservative and optimistic traffic shapes so you and procurement can see the math behind the slab recommendation. High-level summary below — please skim and I can walk through numbers on a quick call.

Assumptions (short):
- Workload: conversational QA for clinical workflows, average request tokens 110, average generated tokens 220 (including system tokens).
- Peak concurrency window: 08:00–10:00 PT (peak 35% of daily traffic), multi-region active in failover only.
- SLO target: p95 latency <= 200ms for short (<=256 token) completions; p99 budgeting for long tails.
- Model baseline: warm KV cache, quantized 4-bit variant (q4) of the selected open transformer.

Modeling results (quick):
- Expected sustained tokens/sec at peak (client-side): ~58k tokens/s across fleet for 99th percentile day in Q1 post-launch (see sheet "PeakCalc").
- Per-GPU effective median throughput (q4, 32-token prompt chunking): ~2.8k tokens/s for p95 <= 200ms; p95 headroom reduces throughput to ~2.1k tokens/s.
- Slab recommendation: reserve 22 GPU units (committed pool) + 4 burst GPUs for runway, which maps to ~49% safety corridor against the modeled 99th percentile daily peak.

Open questions we used in the model (please confirm):
1) Monthly token commitment range (you mentioned 12M–20M tokens/mo on call; I used 18M in the conservative case).
2) Expected request distribution (ratio short vs long sessions).
3) Any strict regional latency requirement (we modeled US-only with failover).

Next steps: if these assumptions align, Ben will surface the per-GPU token math and Priyom will propose a canary ramp schedule + SLA tweak options for the contract.

Attachments: argo_capacity_model_v1.xlsx (xlsx) — contains detail sheets: PeakCalc, PerGPU, SLA-Scenarios.

Thanks,
Mina
Sr. Solutions Lead, Redwood Inference

Thanks Mina — this is helpful and much clearer than the spreadsheet we tried to build in-house. A few clarifications from our side before we loop legal/procurement: 

- The token commit I quoted on the call was 15M–25M tokens/mo (we were still consolidating a forecast). We can agree to an 18M committed starting month if the slab and pricing match the SLA targets.
- On latency: we need p95 <= 200ms for our triage flows, but our longer post-processing flows can tolerate up to 500ms p95. In your model, does the 200ms band cover both directions (request + generation) or only generation?
- For safety: procurement would prefer a 30% headroom buffer over our 99th percentile peak rather than a fixed GPU count. Is that expressible in your model?

Sara — quick technical follow-up, pulling out the kernel math so the procurement side has something deterministic. Mina's sheet is great; a couple of clarifications below and an alternate view you might prefer (safety %).

Clarifications:
- The "<=200ms" p95 in Mina's conservative run is end-to-end generation latency assuming warm cached KV and single-turn responses <=256 tokens. It does not include extra client-side post-processing. If you need both request encoding + generation under 200ms, we should tighten the per-GPU throughput and increase headroom.

Per-GPU effective throughput (q4 variant) used in the model: 
- Baseline (median): 2,800 tokens/s
- p95 adjusted (accounts for queuing & larger KV hits): 2,100 tokens/s
- We assume autoscaling latency budget consumes ~15% of throughput in peak microbursts; that is baked into the per-GPU p95 figure above.

Options to express safety:
A) Fixed GPU cushion: Mina's sheet -> 22 committed + 4 burst GPUs (~18% absolute capacity cushion).
B) Percentage safety corridor: model 30% over modeled 99th percentile peak — that raises committed GPUs to 26 and suggests a 3-week planned capacity buffer before contract anniversary.

Practical recommendation for ArgoHealth given your stated constraints: go with option B (30% safety corridor) for Q1 launch to bake in traffic volatility, then re-evaluate after 6 weeks of telemetry. That maps to: 
- Commit: 26 GPUs (q4-optimized)
- Burst pool: additional 6 GPUs available on-demand for critical microbursts
- Canary ramp: day 0 -> 10 GPUs, day 7 -> 18 GPUs, day 21 -> full commit (26) assuming no SLO regressions.

Operational notes:
- We'll enable prefix/KV caching on the triage flows; that pushes effective tokens/s up ~12% in stable state.
- Fallback policy: if p95 > 220ms for more than 10 minutes, route new requests to a lower-cost smaller-context model with transparent header so logs show degraded-quality fallback.

I can run a quick simulation with your exact expected short/long session split if you share the ratio — Mina, Priyom, can you sync with procurement on the commitment wording?

-Ben

Thanks everyone — looping in the operational playbook and next steps so procurement has concrete deliverables for the contract. Quoting key lines from the thread for the SOW: 

- Commitment mapping (per Ben recommendation): commit 26 q4-optimized GPUs; burst pool 6 GPUs (on-demand).
- Canary schedule: 0 -> 10 -> 18 -> 26 over 21 days with telemetry gates at day 7 and day 14.
- SLA language to propose to legal: p95 latency <= 200ms for triage flows (<=256 tokens), with an SLA credit band if sustained p95 > 220ms for >30 minutes during peak windows.
- Headroom: 30% safety corridor applied to modeled 99th percentile peak; we will reconcile actual telemetry at day 45 and propose an adjustment (up or down) with 30 days notice.

Action items for ArgoHealth procurement:
1) Confirm committed token band (we used 18M/mo in the conservative run; you indicated 15–25M). Please confirm final starting commit.
2) Approve canary schedule and PO milestone dates (we will tie billing milestones to each canary gate).
3) Return signed commercial term draft; we'll attach the SLA appendix with the p95 definition and failure modes.

I'll produce an updated "SLA & Capacity Exhibit" to attach to the contract by EOD tomorrow once you confirm the committed token target.

Priyom Das
Head of Dedicated Deployments, Redwood Inference
